title: Hard-deleting a published provider re-enables BYOK fallback
justification: The mechanism is real and exactly as described. deleteProvider (adminService.ts:394-459) has no revision>0 / published-state guard — only lockProvider, revision/draft-token CAS, and blocking model dependents — and the repository deleteProvider (platformAiCatalog/index.ts:90-96) hard-deletes the platformAiProviders row. The runtime fail-closed control (runtimeAdapter.ts:395-402) depends entirely on that row surviving with revision>0: on a snapshot miss it calls getProviderByKey and only throws the fail-closed ProviderDisabled error when known.revision>0, otherwise NotFound. loadCurrentAiCatalogSnapshot (catalogAuthority.ts:56) selects FROM platformAiProviders WHERE revision>0, so archive keeps the tombstone (row survives, status archived) while hard-delete removes it. initModelRuntimeFromDB (ModelRuntime/index.ts:571) swallows PLATFORM_NOT_FOUND and falls back to initUserModelRuntimeFromDB (user BYOK, no platform allowlist hooks). So archive fails closed but hard-delete re-opens ungoverned BYOK — the exact asymmetry claimed, and the code comment at runtimeAdapter.ts:396-397 documents the tombstone intent that hard-delete defeats. I moderate CRITICAL to HIGH: concrete model access still requires the user to independently hold BYOK credentials for the same provider key, and the path discloses no platform secret (secrets cascade-delete) and destroys no audit evidence (revisions retained, audit appended). It is a real, prod-reachable governance/authorization fail-open, bounded by that precondition.
decisiveEvidence: runtimeAdapter.ts:398-402 — `const known = await repository.getProviderByKey(providerKey); if (known && known.revision > 0) { throw new AiCatalogProviderDisabledError(providerKey); } throw new AiCatalogNotFoundError();` — after adminService deleteProvider hard-deletes the row (repository index.ts:92 `db.delete(platformAiProviders)`), getProviderByKey returns undefined, so the fail-closed branch is skipped and NotFound triggers BYOK fallback at ModelRuntime/index.ts:571.
correctionNote: Finding's code mechanism, cited lines, and impact chain are all accurate. Only the CRITICAL label is slightly overstated: the BYOK bypass yields real ungoverned model access only when the user independently possesses their own credentials for that provider key (e.g. a residual/self-built AiProvider row previously shadowed by managed AI), and the hard-delete does not disclose the platform's governed secrets or destroy audit/revision evidence. That precondition and the absence of secret/evidence compromise place it at HIGH rather than unconditional CRITICAL.

title: Destructive jobs become runnable before their required audit record exists
justification: The enterprise retention/export services enqueue a destructive job and only afterward append the required audit record, with no wrapping transaction (services are built on ctx.serverDB and neither file contains a db.transaction call), so each step auto-commits independently. PlatformJobModel.claimNext selects pending jobs with no scheduling delay, and a persistent poller (ensurePlatformAuditRetentionWorkerStarted, 3s interval) runs whenever ENABLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN is set — AIHub's deployment mode. The retention worker proceeds to delete evidence for a pending run (retentionWorker.ts:488, 596-644) and the export worker materializes S3 evidence (exportWorker.ts:243-275) without verifying that the request-audit exists or that run.jobId is linked. If the required append fails — or, more realistically, if the API process is killed/redeployed between the enqueue commit (line 205/284) and the append (line 221/318) so the compensation catch never runs — irreversible evidence destruction or sensitive-evidence materialization occurs with the required request-audit record permanently missing. This breaks the code's own declared fail-closed invariant in a compliance/legal-hold audit subsystem, which makes it CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: retentionService.ts:205 `const { job } = await this.jobsModel.enqueue(...)` commits before retentionService.ts:221 `await appendAuditAccessLog(this.db, { ... required: true, ... })`, with no db.transaction wrapping (grep for `db.transaction` in retentionService.ts/exportService.ts returned nothing); retentionWorker.ts:417 `claimNext` + :488 pending->running then deletes.

title: Same-epoch governance fallback can restore permissions after a restrictive policy commit
justification: The mechanism is real and confirmed in code: the cache/LKG epoch (service.ts:45-51) is a best-effort invalidation counter, NOT derived from the authoritative DB revision that publishGovernance commits. Invalidation is decoupled and swallowing (adminService.ts:165-178; the Redis publisher never throws and doesn't incr when Redis is degraded), so a restrictive commit can succeed with the scope version left unchanged. getLastKnownConnectorGovernanceIfCurrent (service.ts:147-148) then returns the stale snapshot whenever epoch matches, and resolveConnectorGovernance (resolve.ts:23-24) returns it on authoritative-read failure instead of DENIED — a genuine fail-open in a control the design explicitly intended to be fail-closed. However, CRITICAL overstates reachability: it needs a compound, non-attacker-controllable failure (lost invalidation on the last restrictive commit AND a sustained governance DB read outage past the 30s resolvedCache TTL). The most common single-process Redis-disabled deployment is unaffected (in-memory publisher reliably bumps the epoch and never throws), and healthy-DB operation always returns the current policy directly. Real security fail-open, but gated behind infrastructure degradation, so HIGH not CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: service.ts:147-148 `if (!epoch || epoch === 'unavailable' || epoch !== lkg.epoch) return null; return lkg.resolved;` — the epoch is only the best-effort invalidation counter (readCacheEpoch, service.ts:45-51), and adminService.ts:165 wraps invalidation.publish in a swallowing try/catch after the DB commit, so a lost invalidation leaves epoch matching a stale permissive LKG that resolve.ts:24 returns.
correctionNote: Finding's mechanism and compound scenario are accurate, but severity is overstated. It is not directly prod-reachable/attacker-triggerable: it requires (1) the restrictive commit's best-effort invalidation to be lost (Redis down/disabled/partial at that instant) AND (2) a sustained authoritative governance DB read failure beyond the 30s resolvedCache TTL before any successful resolve refreshes the LKG. In the common single-process/Redis-disabled deployment the in-memory publisher always bumps the epoch and never throws, so the fail-open cannot occur; and during normal healthy-DB operation the resolver returns the current restrictive policy directly, never reaching the LKG path.

title: Disable commits a tombstone without making runtime reload pending
justification: The disable transaction writes status:'disabled', activationRevision:null (publicationService.ts:1326-1332), whereas the publish path writes status:'pending_restart' + activationRevision:nextRevision (publicationService.ts:976/994). getAuthSnapshotStatus computes pendingRestart exclusively from rows WHERE status='pending_restart' with non-null activationRevision (systemService.ts:205-212, 255-296), so a pure tombstone yields pendingRestart:false. The running Better Auth config is process-cached: src/auth.ts:7-16 reads getInitializedIdentityProviderRuntimeArtifact() once at module eval, and define-config.ts:130-132 filters enabled!==false against that cached startup snapshot with no per-login DB recheck. The only SIGTERM/restart path (restartController.schedule) is reachable only via requestRestart, which is gated on pendingRestart/restart.supported (IdentityProviderPage.tsx:138,239; systemService.ts:374-379) — all false for a tombstone. Thus a compromised provider keeps accepting logins after admin-confirmed disable, with no in-product restart signal or action, until an external process restart. No compensating control (no auto-restart on divergence, no per-request enabled recheck) mitigates it. This is a failure-to-revoke of an authentication path and warrants CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: publicationService.ts:1332 sets `status: 'disabled'` (with activationRevision:null) while systemService.ts:212 filters `.where(eq(platformIdentityProviders.status, 'pending_restart'))` — the tombstone can never enter the pending-restart set, so pendingRestart stays false and IdentityProviderPage.tsx:239 never renders the Restart button.

title: Group-to-role reconciliation fails open and preserves revoked privileges
justification: The code behavior claimed by F2 is accurate: applyGroupRoleMappingToUser fails open on both the incomplete-seed path (groupRoleMapping.ts:88-93 returns {skipped:true} without replacing roles) and on any exception (lines 101-108 swallow and return {skipped:true}), while reconcileIdentityProviderGroupRoles (groupRoleMappingRuntime.ts:59) discards that result and the Better Auth databaseHooks (define-config.ts:262/277/301) additionally wrap the call in swallowing try/catch. So a failed demotion never blocks or downgrades the session, and a deprovisioned user retains their prior role (e.g. identity_admin). This is a genuine fail-open on a privilege-revocation path with no compensating control (RBAC is only reconciled at login, never re-checked per request). However CRITICAL overstates it: in the normal path the demotion works correctly (resolveMappedPlatformRoles drops the removed group and replaceGlobalUserRoles removes identity_admin), so the bug only manifests when a transient DB/seed fault coincides with the deprovisioned user's reconciliation. Revocation is inherently login-triggered/eventual in this design and exposure is time-bounded (next successful login demotes), making this a serious fail-open (HIGH) rather than a deterministic auth bypass (CRITICAL).
decisiveEvidence: groupRoleMapping.ts:101-108 `catch (error) { console.error(...'apply failed (non-blocking)'...); return { applied: [], skipped: true }; }` combined with groupRoleMappingRuntime.ts:59 `await applyGroupRoleMappingToUser(...)` discarding the result — no failure ever reaches the session decision.
correctionNote: Severity corrected CRITICAL→HIGH. The finding is factually correct about the fail-open but overstates reachability/severity: it is not a deterministic auth bypass — it requires a transient DB/seed fault to coincide with the deprovisioned user's login reconciliation (the normal path demotes correctly), and revocation is inherently login-triggered/eventual with a bounded exposure window.

title: One invalid provider causes valid tombstones to be discarded before LKG fallback
justification: The described code mechanism is real: loadDatabasePayload reads tombstones into tombstoneGenerations then throws SECRET_UNAVAILABLE (startupSnapshot.ts:236) if a selected live provider lacks a secret; the outer catch (line 446) discards the whole candidate including the validated tombstone, and fromLkgPayload (lines 316-353) reloads the pre-tombstone LKG with tombstoneGenerations:[] and re-materializes every old-live provider. The LKG never persists tombstones (toLkgPayload maps only payload.rows), so a fallback to an old LKG genuinely resurrects a revoked provider. But the finding overstates reachability/severity: (1) the named 'discovery unavailable' trigger fails CLOSED, not open — the LKG path re-runs discovery for all providers at line 457, so provider B's discovery failure rejects that Promise.all too and yields break_glass (proven by the test at startupSnapshot.test.ts:363). (2) The 'missing secret' trigger needs abnormal DB state: IdP secrets are never revoked (secretStore.ts:100 only sets revokedAt:null) and only deleted when a provider has no published revision (adminService.ts:262-267), while publish validates secret presence (publicationService.ts:922) — so a published live provider always has its secret under normal operation. The defect is a real defense-in-depth gap in revocation convergence, but the specific resurrection path requires corrupted/tampered DB state, not normal operation, making CRITICAL an overstatement.
decisiveEvidence: startupSnapshot.ts:457 `oidcMetadata: await discovery.discover(provider.issuer)` inside the LKG-fallback enrichRuntimeProviders — the LKG path re-discovers ALL providers, so the finding's 'discovery unavailable' trigger fails closed to break_glass rather than resurrecting the tombstone; combined with fromLkgPayload's `tombstoneGenerations: []` (line 352).
correctionNote: Codex overstates reachability: the 'discovery endpoint unavailable' trigger it cites does not cause resurrection — the LKG fallback re-runs discovery for every provider (startupSnapshot.ts:457) so B's discovery failure also fails the LKG path into break_glass. The only working trigger (a published live provider lacking a secret at startupSnapshot.ts:236) is not reachable in normal operation because IdP secrets are never revoked and are only deleted when no published revision exists (adminService.ts:262-267), and publish validates secret presence (publicationService.ts:922); it needs corrupted/manually-tampered DB state. The core coupling defect (LKG carries no tombstone memory, so any co-provider failure that discards a validated tombstone reverts to a stale LKG that resurrects the revoked provider) is real and worth fixing, but severity is MEDIUM given the abnormal precondition, not CRITICAL.

title: The expand-only migration gate permits destructive schema changes
justification: The factual claims are all accurate. verifyExpandOnlyPostBaselineSql (migrations.ts:236-255) only builds two regexes per protected table — DROP TABLE and ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO — so ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE narrowing, DROP CONSTRAINT, and schema-qualified DROP TABLE public.users all pass. The DROP TABLE regex requires the table literal to immediately follow `DROP TABLE [IF EXISTS] `, so `public.` breaks the match. runner.ts:145-148 uses this narrow result directly as the 'expand-only' verdict, and the other runner probes (row-count is COUNT(*), foreign-key checks named FKs) would not catch a dropped non-FK column. So the 'expand-only' name over-promises relative to the implementation — a genuine, confirmed correctness gap. However, CRITICAL is overstated: this is a CI/tooling defense-in-depth verification gate, not a production runtime control. It does not itself cause data loss, bypass auth, destroy evidence, or disclose secrets; harm only arises if an independently-authored destructive migration slips through this false-negative AND is deployed, and the checked SQL is reviewed upstream/official drizzle migration text. That maps to HIGH (serious correctness/state-loss risk in a gate that under-verifies), not CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: scripts/enterprise/verify-migration/migrations.ts:244 `const dropTable = new RegExp(\`DROP\\s+TABLE\\s+(?:IF\\s+EXISTS\\s+)?["']?${table}["']?\`, 'i');` and :248 the RENAME regex are the only two destructive-op checks; no DROP COLUMN / ALTER COLUMN TYPE / DROP CONSTRAINT handling exists.
correctionNote: The finding is technically correct but mislabels severity. It is a false-negative in a CI verification gate (defense-in-depth over upstream/official migration SQL), not a direct production data-loss or auth-bypass vector. Data loss requires a separately-authored destructive migration to pass this gate AND be deployed through the normal rebase/review pipeline, so trueSeverity is HIGH, not CRITICAL. DROP COLUMN being the most common destructive operation yet uncaught is what keeps it at HIGH rather than MEDIUM.

title: Rebase gates treat failure to inspect the worktree as no mutation
justification: The literal code claim is accurate: detectAutofixMutation (gates.ts:238) returns `status.code === 0 && status.stdout.length > 0`, and runProcess resolves (never throws) with a numeric code, so a nonzero `git status` becomes `false` — indistinguishable from a successfully-inspected clean worktree. Both command-gate callers (line 284 and line 420) only fail when the value is `true`, so a failed inspection silently passes. This is a genuine fail-open robustness gap. However CRITICAL severity is badly overstated: this is internal upstream-rebase CI/dev tooling, not a production runtime path — no data loss, auth bypass, evidence destruction, or secret disclosure. detectAutofixMutation is a SECONDARY guard on top of the primary exit-code check; for a false-green to occur a benign lint/test/type-check command must simultaneously exit 0, actually mutate the tree, AND corrupt git metadata so `git status` fails — a contrived triple coincidence, further mitigated by GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 and a fail-closed manual-conflict-review gate in the same pipeline. Note also the cited line 403 points at the vitest-missing-placeholder fail-closed branch, not a mutation-check path (the real second call site is line 420), a minor citation drift.
decisiveEvidence: scripts/enterprise/upstream-rebase-ci/gates.ts:238 — `return status.code === 0 && status.stdout.length > 0;` (a nonzero git status → false → treated as "no mutation")
correctionNote: Code behavior is real, but severity is overstated. It is a fail-open robustness gap in internal rebase-CI tooling, not a CRITICAL security/data-loss defect. Exploitation requires a benign gate command to exit 0 while both mutating the worktree and corrupting git metadata so `git status` fails — a contrived precondition. Impact is a false pass in a secondary guard, with a fail-closed manual-review gate and the primary exit-code check still present. The line-403 citation is a drift (actual second call site is line 420).

title: Path-boundary validation can pass after scanning no files
justification: All four cited lines match the source exactly: walk() swallows readdir errors and returns accumulated files (check-path-boundaries.ts:39-45), each scan root is optional via try/catch (65-71), the command exits 0 whenever violations.length===0 even with zero payloads (89), and the adapter synthesizes filesScanned=1 when code===0 (pathBoundaries.ts:96). That synthesis genuinely defeats the coverage guards it was meant to satisfy — both the adapter's own filesScanned>0 pass-condition (line 42) and the schema's filesScanned>0 requirement (schemas.ts:281,293) — so a zero-coverage scan can be recorded as 'passed'. The underlying fail-open is therefore real. But CRITICAL is wrong: this is a CI/readiness architectural-boundary gate, not a runtime security control, so failure yields false assurance rather than data loss / auth bypass / evidence destruction / secret disclosure. Reachability is also bounded — it needs an abnormal condition (wrong CWD or all roots missing) to produce zero files, and the fabricating collector adapter has no caller or test invocation anywhere in the repo.
decisiveEvidence: scripts/enterprise/production-readiness/adapters/pathBoundaries.ts:96 `filesScanned: filesScanned > 0 ? filesScanned : code === 0 ? 1 : 0,` — fabricates 1 exactly when check-path-boundaries.ts:89 `if (violations.length === 0) { … process.exit(0); }` fires with 0 files, defeating the schemas.ts:293 `value.filesScanned < 1` coverage guard.
correctionNote: Code behavior is exactly as described, but severity is overstated. It is a CI/production-readiness hygiene gate (enterprise import-boundary check), not a prod security control, so no data loss/auth bypass/secret disclosure. The zero-coverage state requires misconfiguration (wrong CWD or missing roots), and the fabricating collectPathBoundaryEvidence adapter is exported but never invoked by any in-repo caller or test, so live reachability is limited. Correct severity: MEDIUM (real, bounded false-assurance / evidence-integrity weakness).

title: Draft-only commits permanently engage the refresh lock
justification: The freshness gate requires the published `revision` to strictly advance (AgentDetailView.tsx:66 `if (fresh.identity.revision <= baseline.identity.revision) return false;`), but assignment upsert/remove (adminService.ts:385/:414) and pinned rollout rollback (rolloutService.ts:622) commit via `updateDraftCas`, which only increments `draftSequence` and never touches `revision` (repository index.ts:253-256). Because the draft token is derived from both fields (publication.ts:50/:54), the refetched detail carries a changed token but an equal revision — exactly the case `isAgentDetailFresh` rejects. The client calls `lock.markCommitted` then `lock.commitWrite`, so `refresh` (useRefreshLock.ts:142-149) rejects the refetch, pins `refreshFailed=true`, and disables every write on the surface; `retryRefresh` re-runs the same failing predicate, so only a full page reload recovers. useRefreshLock.test.ts:126 explicitly locks in this stale behavior. Reachable in normal admin use with no unusual precondition; not CRITICAL since server writes still succeed and there is no data loss, but it consistently bricks a core admin flow, warranting HIGH.
decisiveEvidence: AgentDetailView.tsx:66 `if (fresh.identity.revision <= baseline.identity.revision) return false;` vs repository index.ts:253-256 `updateDraftCas` setting only `draftSequence: params.expectedDraftSequence + 1` (revision unchanged) used by adminService.ts:385 upsertAssignment.

title: The UI publishes and edits an arbitrarily ordered version
justification: The finding accurately describes the code. Version IDs are random nanoids (idGenerator -> `pav_<random>`, non-time-sortable), and the repository's `listExactVersions` orders by `asc(platformAgentVersions.id)`, so the `versions` array is arbitrary w.r.t. creation order. The client (`collectPages` in useAdminAgents.ts) concatenates pages without re-sorting. `useAgentEditor.ts:22` uses `snapshot.versions[0] ?? current`, so the `current` fallback is unreachable whenever any version exists (it is undefined only when versions is empty), and `AgentDetailView.tsx:82` defines `const latest = snapshot.versions[0]` and publishes `latest.id`. The client's own `applyAppendVersion` prepends the new version to index 0, proving the intended invariant is `versions[0]=newest` — but that invariant only survives in a live session; any fresh server read (page reload / SWR revalidate) reverts to arbitrary asc(id) order. This makes it realistic for the editor to seed a draft from an arbitrary old version (also producing a bad `nextVersion` number) and for the Publish button to deploy an arbitrary historical version org-wide. The only imprecision is the phrase "without defining an order" — there is an asc(id) order, just not a meaningful/creation one — which does not change the substance. HIGH (not CRITICAL) because it requires an explicit admin save/publish click gated by a reason modal, with no auth bypass or evidence destruction.
decisiveEvidence: packages/database/src/repositories/platformAgentCatalog/index.ts:351 `.orderBy(asc(platformAgentVersions.id))` over random `pav_<nanoid>` IDs, while client assumes newest-first: AgentDetailView.tsx:82 `const latest = snapshot.versions[0]` -> `actions.publish(latest.id)` and useAgentEditor.ts:22 `const version = snapshot.versions[0] ?? current`.

title: Disabling managed agents leaks materialized clones into ordinary local-agent lists
justification: The code behavior is exactly as claimed: with ENABLE_PLATFORM_MANAGED_AGENTS off, mergeAvailableAgents (line 201), mergeSidebarList (241), and mergeSearchResults (268) short-circuit to legacy/base without reading listMaterializedAgentIds, so previously-materialized rows are not stripped. But the HIGH "leak of managed content" framing is overstated. This is not an isolated list bug — the entire enterprise agent-catalog layer flag-gates identically and disengages together when off: the effective resolver returns [] (effectiveResolver.ts:146), the default-inbox resolver returns null (defaultInbox.ts:45), and, decisively, the ordinary edit/delete mutation guard is a documented no-op when off (managedPlatformAgent.ts:84,150). The materialized row is owner-scoped (listMaterializedAgentIds(userId) / getPlatformAgentIdsByMaterializedAgentIds(userId,…)) and non-secret (buildLocalAgentRow persists no secrets, materialization.ts:287-306), the runtime config authority is always the pinned snapshot not the row (materialization.ts:308-341), and re-enabling the flag re-hides the row — so the effect is bounded, reversible, and requires a deliberate full-feature rollback (flag defaults OFF). Turning off the whole feature reverting artifacts to legacy behavior is expected graceful degradation, not a governance bypass. The finding's own proposed fix (strip materialized IDs from legacy lists when off) would make the user's own agents and conversation history inaccessible — arguably a worse defect — since the platform item is also not shown when off.
decisiveEvidence: managedPlatformAgent.ts:84 `if (!parseEnterpriseFeatureFlags(process.env).ENABLE_PLATFORM_MANAGED_AGENTS) return;` — the edit/delete guard is also a no-op when off, showing the whole managed layer (not just lists) disengages by design; combined with materialization.ts:290 buildLocalAgentRow persisting no secrets and owner-scoped userId throughout.
correctionNote: Code behavior is accurately described, but severity is overstated: the effect is owner-scoped, non-secret, reversible on re-enable, and only occurs on a deliberate full-feature-flag rollback. It reflects a uniform, documented architecture where disabling the flag reverts the entire managed system to legacy behavior (all guards/resolvers no-op), not a targeted list-projection defect. The proposed fail-closed fix would hide the user's own agents and message history and contradict the rest of the layer's flag-off behavior.

title: User timeline bypasses the conversation-evidence permission and disabled policy
justification: All four claims verified against the real enterprise code. In apps/server/src/enterprise/routers/admin/audit.ts:243 `timeline` is registered on `auditRead` (AUDIT_READ), whereas every other conversation surface (conversations.get/list/messages, lines 201/209/217) uses `auditConversationRead` (AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ). The service `listUserTimeline` (adminAuditService.ts:808-820) loads the policy only to read `maxListWindowDays` and never calls `assertConversationAccessEnabled`, unlike the three sibling conversation methods (lines 468/522/618). The model query (auditConversation.ts:513-536) returns topic ids, sessionIds, titles, and timestamps; titles are only secret-masked, not withheld. The UI gates the same data on AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ (ConversationUserPage.tsx:70/102). withPlatformPermission does an exact includes() check with no hierarchy, and the default AUDITOR/USER_ADMIN/AI_ADMIN/IDENTITY_ADMIN roles hold AUDIT_READ but NOT AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ (roles.ts; `platform_audit:conversation_read:all` does not match the `:read:` filter used to build readOnlyPlatformPermissions, verified via node). So a privileged auditor lacking conversation-read can enumerate any user's conversation titles/topic ids/session ids, and the endpoint keeps returning them even when contentAccessMode is `disabled` — a genuine authorization + policy boundary bypass. Severity HIGH (not CRITICAL) is correct: it discloses conversation metadata/titles across all users, not full message bodies, secrets, or evidence destruction.
decisiveEvidence: apps/server/src/enterprise/routers/admin/audit.ts:243 `timeline: auditRead` (AUDIT_READ) vs conversations on auditConversationRead; adminAuditService.ts:808-820 listUserTimeline never calls assertConversationAccessEnabled (present at lines 468/522/618 for other surfaces).

title: Disabling conversation access does not stop conversation exports
justification: The intended kill-switch helper assertConversationAccessEnabled (contentPolicy.ts:28) is applied to the conversation list/detail/message surfaces (adminAuditService.ts:468/522/618) but is entirely absent from the export create, worker, and download paths. In exportService.ts create, the only content-mode check (lines 249-263) is gated on kind==='conversations' && includeMessageBodies, so a metadata-only conversations export or any user_timeline export is created successfully while contentAccessMode==='disabled'. The worker (exportWorker.ts:247-266) uses live policy only for caps and reads bodies from the frozen includesMessageBodies (lines 329/352), so a body-bearing export queued before revocation still executes. Download (exportService.ts:506) checks only the AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ permission, never the current content mode, and the router (audit.ts:333-374) adds no compensating gate. The disabled mode is a platform-wide toggle designed to cut off access without revoking auditors' permissions, so a permission-holding auditor can still enumerate conversation titles/IDs and download pre-revocation bodies — exactly the finding's claim. HIGH rather than CRITICAL because it bypasses a defense-in-depth policy override, not baseline authorization (the actor must already hold the privileged AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ).
decisiveEvidence: exportService.ts:249 `if (params.input.kind === 'conversations' && params.input.includeMessageBodies)` — the ONLY content-mode gate; assertConversationAccessEnabled is never called for exports, unlike adminAuditService.ts:468.

title: Stats-only roles can read global conversation titles
justification: The finding is accurate at every cited point. `rankTopics` (apps/server/src/enterprise/routers/admin/stats.ts:230) is built on `statsProcedure` (stats.ts:32) which requires only `STATS_READ`, and it returns the model result with no output redaction. `PlatformGlobalStatsModel.rankTopics` (globalStats.ts:292-306) selects `topics.title`, `topics.id`, and `topics.agentId` across all users with no owner filter — genuine conversation-derived content, not aggregate stats. The enterprise explicitly gates conversation titles behind `AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ`, which permissions.ts:76 documents as NOT granted to the default auditor, and audit.ts:201-217 requires it for the conversation list/get/messages surfaces. Yet roles.ts:173-181 seeds the default AUDITOR role with all `:read:` permissions (which includes STATS_READ) while the `:read:` filter does not match `conversation_read`, so the auditor holds STATS_READ but is denied AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ. Thus a default-seeded auditor (or any custom STATS_READ role, as the test at stats.test.ts:52 constructs) can read the top-N global topic titles + stable topic/agent IDs while being denied conversation content elsewhere — a real, reachable authorization-boundary bypass. Severity stays HIGH: it crosses the enterprise's single most-protected read boundary via a default role, though it is bounded to top-N (max 100) titles rather than full targeted enumeration.
decisiveEvidence: globalStats.ts:298 `title: topics.title` (and id/agentId) returned by rankTopics under STATS_READ-gated statsProcedure (stats.ts:32,230), while permissions.ts:76 says AUDIT_CONVERSATION_READ is "Not granted to the default auditor package" and audit.ts:201-217 gates conversation titles behind it.

title: Required audit records are written after cancellation and terminal worker commits
justification: The code behaves exactly as claimed and there is no compensating transaction or recovery path. Both cancel services (retentionService.cancel, exportService.cancel) commit domain + job cancellation (and export cancel even deletes the object) before the required audit append, and the retention worker commits runsModel.complete then jobs.complete before appendWorkerOutcome(required:true); appendWorkerOutcome/appendAuditAccessLog only re-throw on failure, they never roll back the already-committed state, and the completion path is not wrapped in db.transaction (the only transaction, line 531, wraps per-batch destructive work and writes no audit row). Because the job is already 'succeeded', the catch path cannot requeue, so a transient append failure permanently loses the required outcome/cancel audit. However, HIGH overstates it: this needs a transient DB failure in a narrow window after commit but during append; the domain run/export row still retains status+counts, the request-time audit still exists, cancel is the destruction-stopping direction, and the loss is a single immutable outcome record rather than evidence destruction or auth bypass. That places true impact at MEDIUM — a real, fix-worthy atomicity/durability gap that is bounded, not a serious state-loss/auth defect.
decisiveEvidence: retentionWorker.ts:654-690: `const completed = await runsModel.complete(...)` then `const jobDone = await jobs.complete(...)` then `await appendWorkerOutcome(db, {... required: true ...})` — three separate non-transactional commits; appendWorkerOutcome (line 398) only `if (params.required) throw error;` without rolling back the already-succeeded job/run.
correctionNote: Finding's code claims are fully accurate (ordering and non-transactionality verified, line numbers match). Severity is overstated: impact is a bounded audit-log-completeness gap gated on a narrow transient-DB-failure window, with domain state (run/export row counts+status) and the request-time audit retained, and cancel being the safe direction — not evidence destruction/state loss/auth bypass. Corrected HIGH -> MEDIUM.

title: Failed cleanup can leave sensitive export objects permanently orphaned
justification: The code facts all hold. safeDelete swallows every deleteObject error (exportWorker.ts:511-520) and the cancel service uses best-effort .catch(()=>undefined) (exportService.ts:699-701). The export row's storageKey is only persisted by complete() under status='running' (auditExport.ts:200-229), so any failure after the object is uploaded (line 385) — checksum/size mismatch (non-terminal, lines 393-406), a cancel race giving completedRow=null (line 424), or a cancel of a running export (exportService.ts:693) — leaves the DB row failed/cancelled with storageKey=null while the deterministic S3 object still exists. Neither retention scan can ever reclaim it: listExportArtifactCandidates filters to status IN ('completed','expired') AND storageKey IS NOT NULL (auditRetention.ts:533,535) and listPendingArtifactPurges requires status='expired' (auditExport.ts:577). uploadArtifact sets no object TTL/lifecycle (exportStorage.ts:113-129), so there is no infra self-healing. The orphaned object holds conversation evidence (message bodies for body-bearing exports) and survives the intended retention/destruction window permanently — a serious durability/compliance guarantee failure for an audit-evidence system. Severity sits on the HIGH/MEDIUM line because it needs a transient S3 delete failure to coincide with a fail/cancel (and some paths attempt deletion twice), but the total lack of any recovery path makes even a rare occurrence permanent, so HIGH is warranted and consistent with sibling findings F5/F7.
decisiveEvidence: packages/database/src/models/platform/auditRetention.ts:533 `inArray(platformAuditExports.status, ['completed', 'expired'])` (+ line 535 `isNotNull(storageKey)`) — the retention candidate scan can never see a `failed`/`cancelled` orphan; and auditExport.ts:577 `eq(platformAuditExports.status, 'expired')` limits the only other recovery scan.

title: Lease expiry can make retention report zero objects deleted after committed destruction
justification: The mechanism is real and every cited line matches. In processExportArtifacts the cursor+counts checkpoint at retentionWorker.ts:1112 commits with exportArtifactsDeleted:0, then object deletes + outbox completion run in purgeExportArtifactObjectsUnderHoldLock (auditExport.ts:467) inside an advisory-lock TX that never checks the job lease, so destruction commits even if the 60s lease (retentionConstants.ts:5) expired during the up-to-50 slow S3 deletes. The post-delete count checkpoint at 1130 then goes through checkpointBatch, whose jobsTx.checkpoint throws AuditRetentionLeaseLostError on a stale owner (retentionWorker.ts:557-560), losing that batch's deletion count. A replacement worker cannot re-credit it: completeArtifactObjectDelete cleared error to null so the row is no longer PENDING and listPendingArtifactPurges skips it, crash recovery explicitly skips count-merge for foreign outboxes (1041-1042), and the keyset cursor already advanced. So the run can complete under-reporting deletions. But this is strictly an accounting/reporting inaccuracy: the objects are correctly and durably destroyed, nothing is orphaned, no wrong deletion, no data loss, no security bypass. It also needs an unusual precondition (storage slow enough that a 50-object batch exceeds the 60s lease, plus a competing worker). That is a bounded correctness defect (MEDIUM), not the HIGH state-loss the label implies.
decisiveEvidence: retentionWorker.ts:1121-1130 — object delete/outbox-complete (via auditExport.ts:467 hold-lock TX, no lease check) commits, then the deletion-count checkpointBatch at :1130 throws AuditRetentionLeaseLostError (checkpointBatch :557-560) when the lease expired; the completed outbox stores no run id and is no longer PENDING (completeArtifactObjectDelete sets error=null, auditExport.ts:614-616), so the count is unrecoverable.
correctionNote: Severity overstated. The finding proves only that the retention run's aggregate exportArtifactsDeleted count can be under-reported after a lease loss; the destruction itself is correct and durable (outbox completed = object deleted), there is no orphaning, no data loss, and no security impact. It also requires slow storage (50 deletes exceeding the 60s lease within one batch) plus a competing worker, an atypical precondition. Corrected to MEDIUM.

title: Serverless deployments can strand connector runtime audits indefinitely
justification: Every factual claim in F2 is accurate. Shared-credential completions are persisted with status/auditStatus 'pending' (runtimeExecutionJournal.ts:195-196); the inline audit delivery failure at runtimeAdapter.ts:375-382 is swallowed and the successful tool result is returned; the only reconciler runConnectorRuntimeAuditBatch has no production caller except the poller, which ensureConnectorRuntimeAuditWorkerStarted disables when process.env.VERCEL_ENV is set (runtimeAuditWorker.ts:33); no serverless scheduler/queue entrypoint exists; the test only exercises the persistent-worker happy path. The ambiguous-outbound case also has no inline audit (the auditShared('failed') guard is skipped once armed+started), so its 'unknown' audit likewise depends on the disabled worker. However, HIGH overstates reachability: the happy-path audit IS delivered synchronously inline, so the worker is only a fallback for transient-delivery failures and ambiguous outbounds; and this only bites on serverless (Vercel) deployments — AIHub's actual production is Docker/self-hosted where the poller runs and the VERCEL_ENV branch never triggers. So the defect is a real, bounded audit-completeness gap rather than a broad state-loss.
decisiveEvidence: runtimeAuditWorker.ts:33 `process.env.VERCEL_ENV` early return (no other caller of runConnectorRuntimeAuditBatch) combined with runtimeAdapter.ts:376-381 catching and logging the inline `deliverJournalAudit` failure while still returning executionResult.
correctionNote: Facts are fully correct. Severity downgraded from HIGH to MEDIUM: happy-path audits are delivered inline synchronously (worker is only a fallback), so stranding requires BOTH a serverless deployment AND a transient audit-delivery failure or ambiguous outbound. AIHub ships as Docker/self-hosted where the poller runs and the VERCEL_ENV path is inert, making the scenario latent rather than reachable in its primary deployment. No user-data loss, auth bypass, or secret disclosure — it is a bounded compliance-evidence-completeness gap.

title: Read-only AI DTOs expose a deterministic credential verifier (fingerprint)
justification: Every factual claim in F1 is verified against real code: aiSecretStateSchema exposes fingerprint (aiCatalog.ts:191), it is embedded in the list (:292) and detail (:322) DTOs, the test fixture accepts it as safe (aiCatalog.test.ts:94), the auditor system role is granted all :read: perms including AI_PROVIDER_READ (roles.ts:84-89,173-181) and the read procedures are gated only by that permission (router :205/:218/:230), and the value really is an unsalted, deterministic truncated hash — sha256:<first 16 hex of SHA-256(JSON.stringify(keyVaults))> (secretManager.ts:27-28) mapped unredacted into the DTO (model:203/:242). So it IS a deterministic, offline-computable credential verifier reachable by a read-only auditor, and it does leak credential reuse across providers/revisions. However, HIGH overstates the impact: the exposure is only to authenticated admin-console principals (the auditor role already has ADMIN_ACCESS), not external/anonymous attackers; the fingerprint is not the secret and offline-guessing only bites the minority case of low-entropy structured credentials (basic-auth username+guessable password, short custom-header tokens) — for the dominant case of high-entropy API keys/bearer tokens a 64-bit unsalted hash gives essentially no attack value; and the attacker must also reconstruct the exact JSON key set/order. This is a real least-privilege / CWE-200/CWE-916 information-disclosure weakness (an HMAC-with-server-key or removing the field would fix it), but its bounded reachability and narrow preconditions make it MEDIUM, not HIGH.
decisiveEvidence: apps/server/src/enterprise/services/aiCatalog/secretManager.ts:27-28 — `const fingerprintSecret = (plaintext: string): string => `sha256:${createHash('sha256').update(plaintext).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)}`;` — an unsalted, deterministic SHA-256 over the raw serialized credential, surfaced unredacted to AI_PROVIDER_READ (auditor) via model mapping fingerprint: provider.secretFingerprint ?? null (aiCatalog.ts:203/242).
correctionNote: The finding's technical claims are all correct; only the severity is overstated. Impact is bounded because disclosure is to a trusted read-only admin role rather than an external attacker, no actual secret/plaintext/ciphertext is exposed, and the offline-verification attack is only practical for the minority of low-entropy structured credentials (basic-auth / short header tokens), not the high-entropy API keys that dominate real deployments. Hence MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: Enabled email-domain allowlisting fails open when the list is empty
justification: Every link in the chain holds. The schema (packages/types/src/platform/authSettings.ts:37-43) accepts emailDomainAllowlist:[] together with emailDomainAllowlistEnabled:true with no cross-field refinement; the matcher isEmailDomainAllowed returns true for an empty list; and the registration guard rejects only when `enabled && !isEmailDomainAllowed(...)`, so enabled+empty evaluates to `true && !true` = false — every email self-registers. No layer prevents the enabled+empty state: the contract reuses the schema verbatim, the server router persists it directly, and the UI handleSave saves it silently (its invalid-domain check no-ops on an empty array). This is a silent fail-open of a registration access control with a misleading 'enabled' toggle, reachable via the natural admin sequence of toggling the switch on and clicking the now-enabled Save button before typing domains. Severity stays HIGH rather than being downgraded because there is zero guard at any layer and the trigger path is common, not an unusual precondition; it is bounded only by requiring openRegistration to be on and creating low-privilege accounts, which keeps it below CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: src/libs/better-auth/plugins/registration-guard.ts:44-46 `settings.emailDomainAllowlistEnabled && !isEmailDomainAllowed(email, settings.emailDomainAllowlist)` combined with authSettings.ts:82 `if (allowlist.length === 0) return true;` — enabled+empty yields `true && !true` = false, so no email is ever rejected.

title: Full-document settings updates allow stale administrators to overwrite security changes
justification: The code facts are exactly as claimed: both contracts (adminAuthSettings.ts, adminSidebarLayout.ts) use full-document input schemas with no expectedRevision/revision token and no CAS — the comments even declare "direct-save; no draft/publish CAS." The model layer (packages/database/src/models/platform/authSettings.ts) persists via unconditional onConflictDoUpdate, so a stale full-document write (openRegistration: true) really does silently overwrite a prior admin's security change (openRegistration: false). The underlying lost-update/no-optimistic-concurrency defect is real and reachable. But the finding overstates severity as HIGH: the scenario requires two trusted IDENTITY_UPDATE admins editing concurrently with one holding a stale document (an unusual precondition, not an external-attacker path), and it is not truly "silent" — the router wraps the write and an audit append in one transaction that records the resulting openRegistration/domain state with the actor (authSettings.ts router lines 51-62), so the regression is detectable and correctable. That makes it a bounded correctness/state-loss issue (MEDIUM), not a HIGH auth-adjacent vulnerability. The sidebar-layout half is pure UI-layout data loss, lower still.
decisiveEvidence: apps/server/src/enterprise/contracts/adminAuthSettings.ts:9 `export const adminAuthSettingsUpdateInputSchema = platformAuthSettingsSchema;` (full document, no revision) combined with packages/database/src/models/platform/authSettings.ts:64 `.onConflictDoUpdate({ set: { ... openRegistration: next.openRegistration ... } })` — unconditional last-writer-wins.
correctionNote: Finding labels HIGH but true severity is MEDIUM: it is a lost-update concurrency defect between two trusted admins (needs concurrent stale-document editing), not an attacker-reachable auth bypass, and the transactional audit append (router lines 51-62) records the resulting security-setting state per actor, so the change is not truly silent and is detectable/correctable.

title: Cancelled and dead secret-rotation jobs cannot be restarted
justification: The code does exactly what F4 claims. Start (coordinator.enqueue) deduplicates by idempotencyKey = `rewrap:d2:${targetKeyId}` and, on the onConflictDoNothing collision against the non-partial unique index on (type, idempotency_key), falls through to select and return the existing row regardless of terminal status (coordinator.ts:97-133). The active-status filter (pending/reserved/running) only skips the in-flight branch; it never creates a new job for a still-active target key. Retry cannot recover the job: the input schema forces expectedStatus: z.literal('failed') (adminSecretRotation.ts:65), and even for a failed job the coordinator additionally requires a failure-ledger row (coordinator.ts:231-242) that cancelled jobs (coordinator.cancel) and dead jobs (worker.ts markClaimedDead, category 'invalid_job_contract') never write. There is no restart method in adminService.ts. The cancel-then-restart flow is a normal admin action and is fully reachable; the only recovery is bumping PLATFORM_SECRET_REWRAP_DOMAIN_SET_VERSION in code and redeploying. It is a serious correctness/state-loss defect (permanently stranded key-rotation operation, no runtime recovery) rather than a security bypass, so HIGH is warranted; note the 'prevent retirement of historical key' phrasing is slightly softened by historicalKeyRemovalReady being a hardcoded false gated externally, but the core 'rotation cannot complete / old-key ciphertext lingers' impact holds.
decisiveEvidence: coordinator.ts:118-133 selects and returns the existing (cancelled/dead) job after onConflictDoNothing against the non-partial unique index (jobs.ts:79 / migration 0117 line 357 `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ("type","idempotency_key")` with no WHERE), while retry is gated by `expectedStatus: z.literal('failed')` (adminSecretRotation.ts:65) plus a failure-ledger requirement (coordinator.ts:242 `if (!ledger) throw new PlatformSecretRewrapConflictError()`).

title: Crashed jobs can exceed maxAttempts and repeat side effects
justification: The code facts are exactly as claimed: PlatformJobModel.claimNext eligibility (job.ts:335-340 and the guarded UPDATE at 373-381) is only status='pending' OR status='running' with expired lease, with no maxAttempts test, and nextAttempt = candidate.attempt + 1 is unconditional (job.ts:361). maxAttempts is enforced only in fail() (job.ts:459-460), and no reaper dead-letters exhausted crashed jobs. So on an uncaught worker-process crash (OOM/SIGKILL/deploy) between claim and fail/complete, the job is re-claimed after lease expiry and attempt grows past maxAttempts — the retry-budget circuit breaker only works on the clean/caught path. However, the finding overstates impact: every real worker wraps execution in try/catch and routes normal errors to jobs.fail(), which correctly enforces maxAttempts and dead-letters at the limit (exportWorker.ts:496-505). Only an uncaught process crash slips past, and the concrete jobs have compensating idempotency: the rollout worker runs a transactional CAS (atomic rollback on crash) and the export worker re-uploads to a deterministic storage key gated by the export-row status, so destructive side effects are not actually repeated. The residual defect is a bounded reliability gap (retry-budget bypass / potential crash-loop that is never dead-lettered), not the data-integrity/side-effect-repetition class that HIGH implies — MEDIUM is the honest severity.
decisiveEvidence: job.ts:335-340 claim conditions have no maxAttempts check and 361 `const nextAttempt = candidate.attempt + 1`, while maxAttempts is enforced only at fail() job.ts:459-460; exportWorker.ts:496-505 shows the caught-error path (`if (failedJob?.status === 'dead')`) does enforce the budget, so the gap is limited to uncaught crashes.
correctionNote: Codex missed that (1) normal errors are caught and routed to fail(), which DOES enforce maxAttempts and dead-letters, so only uncaught process crashes bypass the budget; and (2) the actual jobs are idempotent/transactional (rollout transactional CAS; export deterministic S3 key + export-row status guard), so destructive side effects are not truly repeated. The maxAttempts-on-claim gap is real but its realistic impact is a bounded retry-budget/crash-loop reliability issue, not HIGH-severity side-effect duplication.

title: Admin UI hides revoke for edited providers whose old publication remains live
justification: The two frontend disable guards (IdentityProviderPage.tsx:76-83 and :293-298) both accept only status active/pending_restart/published/error, so a provider whose head is 'draft' shows no Disable button and requestDisable returns early. The backend disable() intentionally supports exactly this case: its docstring (publicationService.ts:1246-1249) and inline comment (:1272-1273) state that after edit/secret-clear the head is draft+activationRevision=null but is 'still tombstoneable', and the method derives publish history from the latest published revision row (:1274-1295), rejecting only disabled/archived heads or never-published providers. The draft state is trivially reachable: adminService.ts:200-220 (update) unconditionally sets status:'draft' on any edit including secret replace/clear, while the previously published revision remains loaded in running instances until a tombstone+restart. There is no alternate UI revoke path (delete throws PLATFORM_IDENTITY_PROVIDER_HAS_PUBLISHED_REVISION at adminService.ts:262-263). So an urgently-needed revocation of a still-live, compromised provider is hidden by the UI — a serious security-response gap, correctly rated HIGH. It is not CRITICAL only because the backend capability exists and a technical operator could invoke the procedure directly.
decisiveEvidence: IdentityProviderPage.tsx:293-298 `const disableable = item.status === 'active' || ... 'error'; if (!disableable) return null;` (excludes 'draft') vs publicationService.ts:1272-1273 comment `After edit/secret-clear the head is draft+activationRevision=null — still tombstoneable.`

title: Successful secret mutations can persist the exact client secret as an audit reason
justification: The technical claim is fully accurate. safeIdentityDeniedReason (identityProviders.ts:114-144) does value-based redaction by comparing the reason against the replacement value and the resolved current secret, but it is wired only as resolveDeniedReason (line 163), which reauth.ts:117-119 invokes solely inside the catch block after reauth fails. On successful (fresh) reauth the mutation runs and adminService.ts writes reason: input.reason verbatim into both success audits (lines 159, 230) and the failure audit (line 109); auditLog.ts:127 persists reason with no redaction (only afterDiff/beforeDiff pass through redactSensitive). The only success-path guard is the contract reasonSchema (contracts/identityProviders.ts:154-162), which uses only the pattern-based containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial — that detector cannot recognize a bare opaque random client secret, so it lands permanently in the append-only log. However, HIGH overstates it: exploitation requires a privileged admin to voluntarily paste the exact opaque secret into a free-text reason field (self-inflicted, atypical), most patterned secrets are already caught, and disclosure is confined to audit-read holders within the admin trust boundary with no attacker-controlled path — a real but bounded secret-hygiene / defense-in-depth gap (MEDIUM).
decisiveEvidence: reauth.ts:117-119 resolves the denied reason only in the catch (`((await params.resolveDeniedReason()) ?? null)`), while adminService.ts:159 writes `reason: input.reason` on the success audit and auditLog.ts:127 stores `reason: params.reason ?? null` with no redaction.
correctionNote: Finding is technically correct but severity is overstated. Reachability depends on an unusual self-inflicted admin action (pasting the raw client secret into the reason field) and only an opaque, unpatterned secret escapes; disclosure stays within the privileged admin/audit-read boundary with no external or attacker-driven path. This is a bounded secret-hygiene/defense-in-depth inconsistency (the denied path is paradoxically better protected than the success path), i.e. MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

title: Auth-setting writes have no CAS and can silently reopen registration
justification: The technical mechanics are exactly as claimed: the platform_auth_settings singleton has no revision column, the update input schema (platformAuthSettingsSchema, .strict()) requires all three fields so the client always sends a full document, and the model computes next.openRegistration = patch.openRegistration ?? current then does an unconditional insert(...).onConflictDoUpdate keyed only on id — no expected-revision predicate anywhere in router, contract, or model. GeneralSettingsPage submits draft.openRegistration (hydrated from stale loaded data) even when only the allowlist is edited, so a stale second writer silently reopens registration under last-writer-wins. This is a real lost-update on a security-relevant control. However, HIGH overstates it: the scenario needs two concurrent privileged admins with overlapping stale windows (unusual precondition, both trusted actors, not an external auth bypass), and every write is recorded fail-closed in the audit log (afterDiff.openRegistration), making the change detectable and recoverable. The absence of CAS is also a documented, deliberate direct-save design choice. It is a genuine but bounded concurrency defect — MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: models/platform/authSettings.ts:54 `openRegistration: patch.openRegistration ?? current.openRegistration` feeding an unconditional `insert(...).onConflictDoUpdate({ target: platformAuthSettings.id })` (lines 57-73), with input schema `.object({...}).strict()` requiring openRegistration (types/platform/authSettings.ts:37-43) — full-document write with no expected-revision CAS.
correctionNote: The finding's code-level claim is fully accurate (no CAS, full-document last-writer-wins, reopen reachable). It overstates severity as HIGH: the scenario requires two concurrent trusted admins with stale state (narrow precondition, not an attacker path), and every write is audited within the same transaction, so the reopen is detectable and recoverable rather than truly silent. Correct severity is MEDIUM.

title: Enabled email allowlisting accepts an empty list as unrestricted
justification: The code claims are fully accurate: the Zod schema (packages/types/src/platform/authSettings.ts:37-43) has no refine rejecting enabled+empty, the model (packages/database/src/models/platform/authSettings.ts:42-76) persists any combination, and the sign-up guard only rejects when `emailDomainAllowlistEnabled && !isEmailDomainAllowed(...)` — where isEmailDomainAllowed returns true for an empty list. Thus enabling the allowlist with an empty list enforces nothing, and the admin UI's handleSave has no non-empty check, so the state is trivially reachable. The issue is a genuine fail-open validation gap on a security control. However HIGH overstates it: the bug only bites under a specific operator misconfiguration (open registration on — the permissive default anyway — plus allowlist enabled but left empty), there is no attacker-driven bypass of a correctly configured system, and the fix is simply entering a domain. That makes it a real-but-bounded MEDIUM rather than a serious HIGH state-loss/correctness defect.
decisiveEvidence: packages/types/src/platform/authSettings.ts:82 `if (allowlist.length === 0) return true;` combined with registration-guard.ts:44-46 `settings.emailDomainAllowlistEnabled && !isEmailDomainAllowed(email, settings.emailDomainAllowlist)` — enabled+empty yields `true && !true` = false, so no email is rejected.
correctionNote: The finding's technical claims are all correct and verified. The only correction is severity: HIGH is overstated. The defect requires operator misconfiguration (allowlist enabled + empty list + open registration on) rather than being an attacker-triggered auth/authorization bypass, and the consequence is bounded to unrestricted self-registration that any entered domain immediately fixes — MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: Global credential updates silently overwrite concurrent edits
justification: The mechanism the finding describes is factually real: the router `update` input (creds.ts:203-211) carries no revision/expectedUpdatedAt, and the model writes with `.where(eq(platformGlobalCredentials.id, params.id))` after `.for('update')` (globalCredential.ts:300-321) with no CAS, while the schema (credentials.ts:57) has only `updatedAt` and no row-version. So last-write-wins / lost-update on the credential row is genuinely present. However, the severity is overstated as HIGH. The flagship security scenario — B silently reverting A's rotated secret key TOKEN via a stale form — is NOT reachable: platform-mode KV forms never pre-fill secret plaintext (platformPrefillKvPairs), empty value fields are dropped (buildKvUpdateValues) and omitted on the wire (EditKVForm.tsx:117-119), and the server treats an empty/absent `values` as metadata-only, keeping the existing secret (adminService.ts:353-355). Thus a stale form cannot revert a secret; only a deliberate re-type rotates it. The genuinely reachable lost update is limited to non-secret metadata (name/description), which the forms always resend from a snapshot — a real but bounded correctness issue that additionally requires two admins editing the same credential concurrently.
decisiveEvidence: packages/database/src/models/platform/globalCredential.ts:320 `.where(eq(platformGlobalCredentials.id, params.id))` (no revision guard after `.for('update')`) confirms the missing-CAS mechanism; src/routes/(main)/settings/creds/features/EditCredModal/editKvFormUtils.ts:28-32 platformPrefillKvPairs emits `{ key, value: '' }` (secrets never carried), defeating the flagship secret-reversion scenario.
correctionNote: Codex overstates severity (HIGH→MEDIUM) and mis-scopes impact. The claimed security-sensitive scenario ("B submits an older form and silently reverts A's rotated secret TOKEN") cannot occur: platform-hosted secret values are never returned to or pre-filled in the edit form, empty secret fields are stripped client-side and treated server-side as "keep existing" (filterNonEmptySecretValues + the Object.keys(submitted).length > 0 guard), so a stale/passive submit leaves the secret untouched. The only reachable lost update affects non-secret metadata (name/description), and it requires two admins editing the same credential concurrently — real but low-consequence, not a HIGH security defect.

title: File credentials have no in-place secret-rotation path
justification: The factual core is correct: there is no in-place secret-rotation path for file credentials. The router `update` input carries only description/id/name/values (creds.ts:203-232), the service `update` throws 'Values can only be updated for KV credentials' for any non-KV type (adminService.ts:347-352), and although the model `update` can rotate an envelope for any type (globalCredential.ts:324-353), no API ever supplies an envelope for a file credential. Grep confirms `createFromStagedUpload` is consumed only by `createFile`, so the sole rotation lifecycle for files is delete+recreate. However, the HIGH severity is overstated: this is a missing capability, not a security or state-loss defect. There is no silent data loss (the admin deletes explicitly), no auth bypass, no secret disclosure; the audit ledger is append-only so history is preserved, and a delete-then-recreate-with-same-key workaround exists under admin control. The real impact is a bounded availability window and loss of ID/revision continuity during rotation — a MEDIUM operational gap. The finding's own fix is framed as an API extension (a feature), confirming enhancement rather than bug.
decisiveEvidence: apps/server/src/enterprise/services/platformGlobalCredentials/adminService.ts:348-351 — `if (existing.type !== 'kv-env' && existing.type !== 'kv-header') throw new PlatformGlobalCredentialValidationError('Values can only be updated for KV credentials');` combined with router update input (creds.ts:205-210) exposing only values/name/description and no staged-upload consumer besides createFile.
correctionNote: Factually accurate but severity overstated: this is a missing rotation feature, not a HIGH security/state-loss bug. No silent data loss, no auth bypass, no secret disclosure; audit history is append-only and a delete+recreate (same key) workaround exists under admin control. Real impact is a bounded availability window plus ID/revision-continuity reset during rotation, i.e. MEDIUM.

title: Hardening migration builds large production indexes while blocking writes
justification: The technical claim is fully accurate: migration 0145 issues plain (non-CONCURRENTLY) CREATE INDEX statements on topics (lines 115, 126) and messages (lines 118, 121), including a GIN trigram index inside a transaction-bound DO block. I confirmed topics and messages are the core upstream LobeHub chat tables (packages/database/src/schemas/topic.ts:24, message.ts:95), not new empty enterprise platform_* tables, so on a populated install the SHARE lock a non-concurrent CREATE INDEX takes will block all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on those tables for the build duration. The scenario is genuinely reachable (guaranteed on any deploy against a populated DB). However, HIGH overstates it: this is a one-time, non-destructive, planned-deploy availability concern bounded to the migration window (reads still work, no data loss, no correctness/state-loss, no security impact) — which fits MEDIUM ("real but bounded") rather than HIGH ("serious correctness/state-loss"). The proposed fix (staged non-transactional migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS) is sound.
decisiveEvidence: packages/database/migrations/0145_platform_db_hardening.sql:118 `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS "messages_user_id_topic_id_created_at_id_idx" ON "messages" USING btree ("user_id", "topic_id", "created_at", "id");` — non-concurrent build on the high-volume upstream messages table (schemas/message.ts:95), taking a write-blocking SHARE lock.
correctionNote: Finding is technically correct but mislabeled HIGH. It is a bounded, one-time, non-destructive migration/deploy availability concern (writes to topics/messages stall during index build), not a runtime correctness/state-loss or security defect; true severity is MEDIUM.

title: Disabled connector mode falsely reports successful disconnection
justification: The code behavior is exactly as claimed: `connectors.ts:70` returns `{ disconnected: true }` when `ENABLE_PLATFORM_MANAGED_CONNECTORS` is off, bypassing the real `UserConnectorOAuthService.disconnect` (userOAuthService.ts:601-631), which otherwise revokes the binding in a transaction, writes an audit entry, and cleans up the token/PKCE secret refs. The `withActiveUserWhenManaged` middleware passes through when the flag is off (managedActiveUser.ts:72-74), so the fabricated-success line is reachable, and the binding/secrets genuinely remain. So the defect is real and confirmed. However, HIGH overstates it: the exploit chain needs a deployment-level env flag toggled OFF (requires a server restart) and later re-enabled; during the OFF window the whole managed-connector runtime is blocked (listManaged returns empty, startAuthorization returns FORBIDDEN), so the stale token is inert and unusable; and the issue is retention/false-success on the user's OWN credential, not an auth bypass, cross-user leak, or evidence destruction. That makes it a genuine correctness/security-hygiene bug of bounded impact — MEDIUM, not HIGH.
decisiveEvidence: apps/server/src/enterprise/routers/user/connectors.ts:70 — `if (!featureEnabled()) return { disconnected: true as const };` returns success without calling the revoking service at userOAuthService.ts:607 `revokeBindingWithPreviousSecret(command.connectorId)`.
correctionNote: The finding is factually correct about the code but overstates severity. Reachability requires an ops-level env-flag toggle (process.env, needs restart), not a routine or attacker-triggered action. While the flag is off there is no active exposure: the connector runtime is blocked and listManaged/startAuthorization deny access, so the un-revoked token cannot be used; the believed-revoked-but-live window only opens after an admin re-enables the whole feature. It affects the user's own credential retention, not an auth bypass or cross-user leak. Also the cited line is 70, not 66 (the quoted code is exact; minor drift).

title: Generic publish failures can strand all connector runtime access in blocked mode
justification: The mechanism is real and the cited lines match: connectorTransitionCanRestore (managedResources.ts:82) is set true only for PlatformRevisionConflictError (l.119) and ManagedResourceCatalogNotReadyError (l.127), and the finally (l.137) cancels only when that flag is true. beginConnectorRuntimeEffectiveStateTransition publishes effective mode 'blocked' before service.publish(), so a generic pre-commit failure (e.g. a DB deadlock inside publishDraft) rethrows at l.135 without cancelling, leaving the effective state blocked while the policy is unchanged — a genuine correctness gap in the cleanup logic. However the finding overstates impact/severity: the transition lease auto-expires after 30s (PX 30_000), and the routine platform.getCapabilities endpoint (platform.ts:83) then republishes the DB-resolved correct mode via CAPABILITY_SCRIPT once the lease no longer EXISTS, self-healing the state. The condition is thus fail-closed (deny, not bypass), bounded, self-healing, and requires a rare generic pre-commit failure — MEDIUM, not the HIGH 'strand all connector runtime access' the title implies.
decisiveEvidence: managedResources.ts:137 `if (connectorTransitionToken && connectorTransitionCanRestore)` (no cancel on generic error) combined with the lease-gated self-heal: runtimeEffectiveState.ts CAPABILITY_SCRIPT `if redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[3]) == 1 then return ... end` invoked by platform.ts:83 publishConnectorRuntimeCapabilityState after the 30s lease (TRANSITION_LEASE_MS = 30_000) expires.
correctionNote: Codex missed the compensating self-heal path: the 30s Redis lease auto-expires and platform.getCapabilities (a routine call) republishes the correct DB-resolved capability mode via CAPABILITY_SCRIPT once the lease is gone. The block is therefore transient, fail-closed, and self-healing — not a persistent strand — so severity is MEDIUM, not HIGH. The finding's own Impact wording ('until another capability publication repairs the persistent effective state') already concedes automatic recovery exists.

title: Production-readiness evidence can pass without assertions
justification: The two code-level claims are accurate. In evaluate.ts:231-240 the guard `input.status === 'passed' && input.assertions && (...)` short-circuits when `assertions` is omitted, so a passed gate with no assertions field falls through to line 242 `return { result: 'passed' }` — directly contradicting the comment "Zero-assertion pass is never allowed." And provenance.ts:91 makes `assertions` optional in the signed payload, while verifySignedProvenance (266-418) never compares assertions and evaluateOneGate only compares `status` (224-227), so the signed assertion summary is never bound to the submitted envelope. However, HIGH overstates the impact: the bypass only affects the overall verdict on the full production-authorized path (evaluate.ts:317-323), which is currently unreachable because the shipped PRODUCTION_TRUST_POLICY has `productionPassEnabled: false` and empty `trustedKeys` (policy.ts:38-42, "production overall pass is impossible until a reviewed public key/issuer is added"). Even once enabled, the Ed25519 signature against the pinned policy — the primary trust anchor — is fully intact and not bypassed; the zero-assertion rule is a defense-in-depth supplement in internal release-gate tooling with no data loss, auth bypass, or runtime surface. It is a real but bounded, latent correctness gap → MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: evaluate.ts:233 `input.assertions &&` — omitting the field short-circuits the guard, and line 242 then returns `{ result: 'passed' }`, so "Zero-assertion pass is never allowed" is bypassable; combined with provenance.ts:91 `assertions: assertionSummarySchema.optional()` and no assertion comparison anywhere in verifySignedProvenance.
correctionNote: Codex's code reading is correct, but it labels a latent, defense-in-depth gap as HIGH. The scenario requires production trust to be explicitly enabled (currently impossible: productionPassEnabled=false, zero trusted keys in the shipped policy), and the cryptographic signature trust anchor remains intact even then — the missing assertion binding only weakens a supplementary evidence check in internal release tooling, not a security or state-loss control. True severity MEDIUM.

title: Failure-drill verification accepts forged aggregate reports
justification: The technical core of F5 is accurate: verifyFailureDrillEvidence (runner.ts:173-182) reads only the stored aggregate `${scenarioId}.json` files and returns records.every(isPassingFailureDrillEvidence); it never re-reads raw vitest reports nor recomputes/compares artifact.sha256, which the schema (contract.ts:12) only format-validates. The fixture buildPassingFailureDrillEvidenceFixture (failureDrillGate.ts:69) hard-codes sha256='b'*64 and the test (upstream-rebase-ci.test.ts:637) confirms these forged aggregates pass. However, the HIGH "accepts forged aggregate reports without any drill having run" severity overstates reachability. The forgery is exercised only through injectedEvidenceDirectory, explicitly commented as a "Test seam" (failureDrillGate.ts:287). The real gate path (gates.ts:381 → failureDrillGate.ts:364-405) freshly collects evidence from real raw reports into a temp dir and additionally gates on suiteFailed and collect.code; enterprise-failure-drills.yml co-locates collect→verify→forbidden-scan in one trusted job and independently asserts each real suite outcome==success (lines 204-208). The uploaded evidence artifact is 14-day record-keeping, not re-verified by any downstream gate, so no production trust boundary consumes externally-forged aggregates. This is a real but bounded integrity-design gap (decorative sha256 provenance never rebound), appropriately MEDIUM, not a HIGH evidence bypass.
decisiveEvidence: runner.ts:181 `return records.every(isPassingFailureDrillEvidence);` — verify reads only aggregate JSON and never rebinds artifact.sha256; but production gate at failureDrillGate.ts:378-405 regenerates evidence via `collect` and fails on `suiteFailed`, so forged aggregates only pass via the test-seam injectedEvidenceDirectory.
correctionNote: Severity corrected HIGH→MEDIUM: the finding treats a genuine integrity-design gap (verify never recomputes/compares the artifact.sha256 digest against raw reports) as a reachable forged-evidence bypass, but it missed that (1) the only path accepting pre-existing aggregates is injectedEvidenceDirectory, explicitly a test seam; (2) both real usages (runFailureDrillsGate production branch and enterprise-failure-drills.yml) freshly collect evidence from actual test reports in the same trusted job and independently gate on suite outcomes/suiteFailed/collect.code; and (3) the uploaded evidence artifact is never re-verified by a downstream consumer, so no production trust boundary ingests forged aggregates.

title: The required migration-upgrade-rollback gate performs no rollback check
justification: The facts are exactly as claimed: migrationGate.ts:178-185 documents "Does NOT claim application-version rollback," yet returns outcome 'passed' with id 'migration-upgrade-rollback' after only upgrade/apply/rerun checks (lines 263-276); gates.ts:93 and rebase-report.ts:493/513-514 make this misleadingly named gate required for migration changes; the test at line 567 locks in upgrade-only behavior (line 615 even asserts the reason must NOT mention app-version rollback). So the gate name promises a rollback check it never performs. However, HIGH overstates it. This is internal upstream-rebase CI tooling, not production code — no data loss/auth/evidence impact. The "false evidence" is mitigated because every emitted reason string honestly disclaims app-version rollback (gates.ts:98, migrationGate.ts:273-274), and the consumed Q03 report requires the 'expand-only' category to pass (Q03_REQUIRED_PASSING_CATEGORIES, enforced lines 107-109), which is the schema-level rollback-safety proxy. True app-version rollback is separately tracked by the app-rollback production gate (F7). This is a contract/naming defect of bounded, non-security impact.
decisiveEvidence: scripts/enterprise/upstream-rebase-ci/migrationGate.ts:184 "Does NOT claim application-version rollback or production-dump overall pass." — yet lines 263-276 return `outcome: 'passed'` with `id: 'migration-upgrade-rollback'`, and rebase-report.ts:513-514 make that gate required whenever migrations change.
correctionNote: Finding overstates severity as HIGH. It is internal CI tooling (not production, not a security bug), the gate's emitted reason strings explicitly and prominently disclaim app-version rollback (only the id is misleading), and the consumed Q03 evidence requires the 'expand-only' category to pass as a schema-level rollback-safety proxy. Actual application-version rollback is covered by the separate app-rollback production gate (F7). This is a MEDIUM naming/contract-clarity defect.

title: The required application-rollback gate is permanently implemented as unavailable
justification: Every factual claim in F7 holds. The spawned baseline loader in baselineMaterialize.ts:182-188 unconditionally prints `ok:false, reason:'baseline-orm-runtime-unavailable'` and exits 1 — even the branch where UserModel.findById is present falls into it — so `baselineExecutable` can never be true (source comment at lines 228-229 states this is intentional). Via appRollback.ts:169 the gate is therefore permanently `unverified`, the integration test (recovery.integration.test.ts:84-86) locks this in, and app-rollback is a REQUIRED_EVIDENCE_GATES member (constants.ts:39) that consequently can never reach `passed`. So the underlying issue is real and not refuted. However, HIGH overstates it: the gate fails SAFE (returns `unverified` + exit 1, never a fake `passed`), giving reviewers no false assurance, and production overall-pass is already independently impossible by design (policy.ts:38-42: productionPassEnabled=false, zero trusted keys), so there is no reachable production harm today. This is an incomplete/stub tooling capability with a test that enshrines it — a bounded completeness/correctness gap, not a security or state-loss defect — hence MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: baselineMaterialize.ts:182-188 unconditionally emits `{ ok: false, reason: 'baseline-orm-runtime-unavailable' }` then `process.exit(1)`, combined with appRollback.ts:169 `else if (!baselineExecutable) status = 'unverified'` — never a fake pass — and policy.ts:38-42 `productionPassEnabled: false` / empty `trustedKeys` making production pass already impossible.
correctionNote: F7's mechanism is accurate, but it is mislabeled HIGH. It is fail-safe (permanent `unverified`/exit 1, never a false `passed`), and production authorization is already independently disabled by PRODUCTION_TRUST_POLICY, so no bad release can be authorized today. It is a MEDIUM tooling capability-gap (a required gate that can never verify its promised app-rollback control, with a test enshrining the stub), not a HIGH security/state-loss defect.

title: Backup verification loads entire databases into memory and performs N+1 queries
justification: The code facts are accurate. The production path reads the entire backup file into memory twice (backupRestore.ts:384 and :445, with `dump` still live for pgRestoreCustom, which itself buffers it again). `digestAllRequiredTables` (invariants.ts:191) does `SELECT ${quoted} FROM "${table}"` selecting every row/column, canonicalizes each row, sorts in JS, and embeds them into a payload it then JSON.stringifies (lines 209-221); this runs on the production path via buildSourceManifestCore->digestAllRequiredTables against the fully restored backup, over tables including platform_audit_logs. Publication-pointer verification (invariants.ts:917-960) is a real N+1, issuing a loop-invariant hasVersion query plus a version lookup per holder row. The production-authorized scope is a reachable CLI (recovery-drill.ts). However, HIGH overstates impact: this is offline release-gating tooling, not the runtime; it fails loudly (OOM/exception -> status failed, exit 1) rather than silently passing a bad backup, and there is no data loss, security bypass, or incorrect-pass. The 64 MiB pg_dump ceiling (ownedPostgres.ts:198) only applies to the harness self-dump of a small seeded fixture, never a production backup, so that sub-claim is inflated. A reachable but bounded efficiency/robustness defect in tooling = MEDIUM, not HIGH.
decisiveEvidence: invariants.ts:209 `const result = await client.query<Record<string, unknown>>(`SELECT ${quoted} FROM "${table}"`);` then lines 210-217 materialize+sort+embed all rows; plus per-row N+1 at invariants.ts:917-960 and double `await readFile(backupAbs)` at backupRestore.ts:384/445.
