correctionNote: Severity overstated as HIGH. It is a scalability/efficiency defect in offline release-gating tooling with a loud-fail mode (no silent incorrect-pass, no data-loss, no security impact), so trueSeverity is MEDIUM. Additionally the pg_dump 64 MiB ceiling sub-claim only affects the harness dump of a small deterministic seeded fixture (production scope reads an external backup file instead, never calls pgDumpCustom), so that part of the finding does not apply at production scale.

title: Alibaba Cloud metadata bypasses the permanent SSRF deny
justification: The code genuinely omits Alibaba Cloud's metadata IP (100.100.100.200) from the METADATA_IPV4 denyset (policy.ts:74-78), which only holds three 169.254.* addresses. isMetadataIp (line 190) therefore returns false for it. In allow-private mode, assertResolvedIpAllowed enforces only the metadata check (line 410); the non-public filter runs solely for public-only mode (line 416-417), so the IP falls through to the allow at line 443. This directly contradicts the code's own stated invariant that cloud metadata is 'permanently blocked in every mode' and that allow-private always blocks metadata. All four cited line numbers match. The scenario is gated behind opt-in allow-private mode plus Alibaba ECS deployment (default public-only mode incidentally blocks 100.100.100.200 via the 100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT range), which keeps it below CRITICAL, but Alibaba deployment is highly plausible for this China-market product and the impact is RAM credential disclosure, so HIGH is warranted.
decisiveEvidence: policy.ts:74-78 `const METADATA_IPV4 = new Set(['169.254.169.254','169.254.170.2','169.254.169.253'])` — Alibaba's 100.100.100.200 is absent; policy.ts:443 `// allow-private: public + private OK; metadata already denied above.` shows the only guard in allow-private mode is the incomplete isMetadataIp check.

title: Write-path redaction ignores known PEM, AWS, and Google secret shapes
justification: The code-level claim is accurate and confirmed: the write-path scrubber `redactString` (redact.ts:134-137) delegates only to `containsSecretValueShape` (redact.ts:109-116), which tests just PREFIXED_SECRET_PATTERN, JWT_PATTERN, and bearer values — never the AWS/GCP/PEM patterns that the shared secretPatterns.ts module defines and that the sibling detector `containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial` (redact.ts:285-288) does test. So `redactSensitive({ note: "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----..." })` returns the PEM verbatim, contradicting the module header's promise that secret material never enters revision/audit payloads and the shared file's stated "keep both consumers in sync" intent. The same gap exists in the assertion helper `containsSensitiveMaterial`. However, the finding overstates severity/reachability: the primary write paths validate free-text at input with the COMPLETE detector — platform agents wrap every field in `safeText`→`addSecretIssue`→`containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial` (platformAgents/common.ts:7-14, 61-77) and IdP validates publicConfig (identityProviders.ts:146) — so PEM/AWS/GCP shapes are rejected before ever reaching the incomplete scrubber there. A narrow reachable path remains (aiCatalog config uses the incomplete `containsSensitiveMaterial` at input, and audit diffs always run through the incomplete scrubber), but the sink in all cases is admin-only privileged storage (platform_audit_logs / platform_resource_revisions), the precondition is a secret placed in a non-sensitively-named free-text field, and the AWS pattern only matches a public access-key ID (not a secret). That is a real defense-in-depth inconsistency and audit-at-rest hygiene defect, but not the HIGH "secret disclosure reachable in prod" the finding asserts.
decisiveEvidence: redact.ts:109-116 `containsSecretValueShape` tests only `PREFIXED_SECRET_PATTERN.test(value) || JWT_PATTERN.test(value)` + bearer; used by `redactString` (135), while `containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial` (285-288) adds `PEM_PRIVATE_KEY_PATTERN.test || AWS_ACCESS_KEY_PATTERN.test || GCP_API_KEY_PATTERN.test`.
correctionNote: Finding is technically correct about redactSensitive but overstates HIGH severity/reachability: the primary revision/audit write paths (platform agents, IdP) reject PEM/AWS/GCP at input via the complete `containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial` detector, so the incomplete scrubber is not the sole defense there; the affected sinks are admin-only audit/revision tables (privileged audience, no cross-boundary disclosure); and the AWS pattern matches only a non-secret access-key ID. Real defense-in-depth/consistency defect → MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: GitHub token detection covers only classic PATs
justification: The technical core is correct: the shared GitHub token detector lists only classic PATs (ghp_[a-z0-9]{20,}) at secretPatterns.ts:60-62, and no other value-shape pattern (JWT/AWS/GCP/PEM/bearer) matches github_pat_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_, or ghr_, so these families slip past containsSecretValueShape (redact.ts:110), maskCredentialsInText (auditCredentialMask.ts:127), and the value-shape leg of containsEnterpriseSecretMaterial. The server redaction layer only re-exports the DB layer, so there is no compensating detector. However, HIGH overstates the impact: two controls the finding omits catch the common cases — key-based redaction (isSensitiveKey) fully redacts tokens stored under credential keys like token/apiKey/oauthAccessToken regardless of value shape, and INLINE_SECRET_ASSIGNMENT_PATTERN (redact.ts:196) catches labeled assignments like `token: github_pat_...`. The genuinely-missed case is a bare GitHub token in unstructured free text reaching admin-visible audit/revision/conversation evidence — a real but bounded defense-in-depth gap within the admin trust boundary, not a cross-tenant or external disclosure. That is MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: secretPatterns.ts:60 — PREFIXED_SECRET_PATTERN = /(?<![\w-])(?:ghp_[a-z0-9]{20,}|sk-[\w-]{19,}[a-z0-9]|xox[baprs]-[a-z0-9-]{10,})(?![\w-])/iu; only ghp_ is listed, so github_pat_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_ are undetected.
correctionNote: Finding overstates severity and reachability. It ignores that (1) tokens stored under sensitive object keys are redacted by isSensitiveKey regardless of value shape, and (2) labeled assignments (token: github_pat_...) are caught by INLINE_SECRET_ASSIGNMENT_PATTERN via the label. Only a bare GitHub token in free text with no label and no sensitive key is actually missed, and exposure is confined to admin-visible audit/revision/evidence surfaces (defense-in-depth), so trueSeverity is MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: Enabling settings policy discards existing registered user preferences
justification: The flag-ON resolver builds each registered path's user layer solely from override rows (effectiveResolver.ts:226) and, when none exists, overwrites the seeded legacy leaf with the built-in/platform default via setByPath (line 253). The service loads only listUserOverrides (effectiveSettingsService.ts:249) and there is no migration backfilling legacy user_settings into user_setting_overrides. Because every override-creating mutation throws PLATFORM_FEATURE_DISABLED while the flag is off, a flag-OFF instance has zero override rows, so enabling ENABLE_PLATFORM_SETTINGS_POLICY (default false, packages/const featureFlags.ts:44) silently reverts every user's registered preferences — fontSize, memory, agent model/provider, approval mode — to defaults on the effective read. This is real, guaranteed, and reachable via the feature's own rollout. I hold HIGH rather than CRITICAL because the persisted user_settings row is preserved (shadowed, recoverable by flipping the flag back), so it is a broad silent effective-value regression, not irrecoverable data destruction.
decisiveEvidence: effectiveResolver.test.ts:269-282 feeds flag-ON legacy {general:{fontSize:16, customUnknown:'keep-me'}} and asserts only the UNregistered customUnknown survives — never that registered general.fontSize survives — proving registered legacy leaves are intentionally overwritten by defaults; mechanism at effectiveResolver.ts:226 `const userOverride = override ? { value: override.value } : null;` + line 253 `effectiveSettings = setByPath(effectiveSettings, path, resolved.effectiveValue);`
correctionNote: Finding's word "discards" slightly overstates: the legacy user_settings row is preserved in the DB (shadowed by defaults on the effective read), not physically deleted, so the reset is recoverable by toggling the flag back off. Impact scope, reachability, and affected-path list are otherwise accurate.

title: Effective-settings cache reuses results materialized from different legacy inputs
justification: The soft cache key (buildSettingsCacheKey, effectiveResolver.ts:276-282) contains only registryVersion/platformRevision/userId/userOverrideRevision and omits legacyUserSettings; getEffectiveSettings (effectiveSettingsService.ts:219-222) returns the whole cached EffectiveSettingsResult on hit without merging the caller's current legacy slice. Runtime adapters demonstrably pass heterogeneous legacy slices for the same user ({memory}, {tool}, {defaultAgent,general,systemAgent,tool,memory}, {defaultAgent,systemAgent,tool}, and full legacy for getUserState), and the resolver's documented contract is that legacy fills unregistered keys — so a hit materialized from a narrow slice loses the unregistered legacy fields of another caller's slice. This is not merely a cross-request race: execAgent (aiAgent/index.ts:1348) deterministically runs resolveEffectiveUserInterventionConfig (personal, legacy {tool}, line 1403) BEFORE agentService.getAgentConfig→getEffectiveDefaultAgentConfig (personal, full legacy, line 1523), so the second read hits the {tool}-materialized cache and returns a defaultAgent config stripped of meta/plugins/params/chatConfig extras. Gated on ENABLE_PLATFORM_SETTINGS_POLICY (the intended AIHub M11 config); DB stays intact and entries expire in 5s, so it is serious silent correctness/state-loss, not CRITICAL.
decisiveEvidence: effectiveResolver.ts:282 `settings:v${registryVersion}:p${platformRevision}:u${userId}:o${userOverrideRevision}` (no legacy component), corroborated by the acknowledged test effectiveSettingsService.test.ts:151 asserting `hit.effectiveSettings` still matches `{general:{language:'en-US'}}` after passing `zh-CN`.

title: Post-publish refresh can overwrite newer policy edits
justification: The code exactly matches the finding: handlePublish calls setSaveState('saved') at line 399 (before await mutate() at 406), which unlocks the editors (editorsLocked = saveState==='saving'||conflict, Select disabled={!canEditPolicy}), then applies setDraft(latest.draft) at line 408 with no epoch capture or shouldPreserveLocalDraftAfterSave guard. The save path by contrast captures submittedEpoch (322) and checks it before applying state (337, 351) and never re-applies the server draft after mutate. A grep confirms line 408 is the only setDraft that is neither epoch-bumped nor epoch-guarded. So a quick admin edit during the post-publish SWR revalidation window is silently reverted. However, this is a client-side race with a narrow window (one revalidation round trip), fully recoverable by re-editing, affecting only unsaved local edits with no persisted-data loss and no security impact, so HIGH overstates it; the true impact is MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: ManagedResourcesPolicyPage.tsx:408 `setDraft(latest.draft);` inside handlePublish's post-mutate block — no submittedEpoch/shouldPreserveLocalDraftAfterSave guard, unlike the save path at lines 322/337/351.
correctionNote: The technical defect is real and reachable, but the claimed HIGH severity is overstated: the loss is a bounded, fully-recoverable client-side state race over a single unsaved edit within one SWR revalidation window — no persisted-data loss, no auth/security impact. True severity is MEDIUM.

title: Secret-bearing versions are permanently persisted despite validation failure
justification: The code does exactly what F1 claims. `createVersion` (adminService.ts:450-486) validates the payload at line 455 but the wrapping `atomicMutation` at 465-484 unconditionally persists the immutable version with `validation: toStoredValidation(validation)` and never inspects `validation.issues` — so a payload with `secret_material_detected` is stored. That issue is error-level (default severity in the `issue()` helper, validator.ts:99; secret checks at validator.ts:536-565 do not downgrade it). Publication DOES block on error issues (publication.ts:87-88 filters `severity === 'error'` and throws), which proves the secret is recognized as blocking yet only publish honors it, not create. `getVersion` (adminService.ts:350-361) returns the full content and resources unredacted, gated only by SKILL_READ (skills.ts:204-205), so a lower-privileged read-only admin can retrieve the credential. The router exposes no version-deletion/purge procedure, and version rows are immutable, so the secret is permanently retained with no scrub path — matching the finding's "no version deletion path" claim. I set trueSeverity HIGH rather than CRITICAL because injection requires a privileged SKILL_UPDATE actor and disclosure is confined to the platform-admin RBAC tier (SKILL_READ), not end-users or cross-tenant; but it is a real bypass of the system's stated "secrets must never enter persistence" contract (redact.ts docstring) with permanent retention.
decisiveEvidence: adminService.ts:465-484 createVersion runs `atomicMutation({... run: async (tx) => { const result = await this.model(tx).createVersion({ actorUserId, ...values, checksum, validation: toStoredValidation(validation) }); ...}})` with no error-level guard — versus publication.ts:87-88 `const errors = result.issues.filter((issue) => issue.severity === 'error'); if (errors.length > 0) throw new SkillCatalogValidationError(errors);`

title: Archiving a built-in override can silently reactivate the bundled skill
justification: The chain is real and reachable. Archiving builds the snapshot via buildPublishedSnapshot(lockedDraft,...) which copies the mutable draft's `enabled` (skillCanonicalize.ts:194), and publication.archive sets builtinOverrideTombstone based solely on skill.allowBuiltinOverride, independent of enabled (publication.ts:147). But the runtime authority requires snapshot.skill.enabled to be true for a tombstone (catalogAuthority.ts:179-183); when enabled is false the archived row hits `!active && !tombstone` and is skipped, so no key reaches builtinOverrideTombstones. readService then deletes builtins only from that tombstone list (readService.ts:223), so the bundled skill silently reactivates. An admin can persist enabled=false on the draft via the standalone updateDraft endpoint (contracts enabled: z.boolean().optional(), updateSkillDraft writes it without publishing) and then archive an active override — restoring an original bundled skill the org intended to suppress. allowBuiltinOverride:true is hardcoded in the production service and the feature is enabled for managed-skills deployments, so this is realistic. Severity HIGH (governance/state-loss: a suppressed builtin skill's capabilities silently return, diverging admin intent from runtime), sitting near the HIGH/MEDIUM boundary because the primary archive-while-enabled path works and the bug needs the specific draft-disable-then-archive sequence.
decisiveEvidence: catalogAuthority.ts:179-183 `const tombstone = revision.status === 'archived' && snapshot.skill.enabled && snapshot.skill.allowBuiltinOverride && snapshot.builtinOverrideTombstone === true;` — gating the tombstone on the mutable, draft-derived `enabled` drops it when enabled=false, and readService.ts:223 `for (const skillKey of snapshot.builtinOverrideTombstones) builtins.delete(skillKey);` then leaves the bundled skill active.

title: Caller-controlled GUCs bypass immutable-version and append-only-audit protections
justification: The technical mechanism is correct: both triggers (0140_...sql:12-13 and 0145_...sql:26-27) gate DELETE solely on current_setting('lobe.allow_platform_*_delete', true) = 'on', and PostgreSQL's current_setting cannot distinguish a transaction-local SET LOCAL/set_config(...,true) from a session-scoped SET — so a caller can enable the setting at session scope and bypass. The legitimate callers correctly use transaction-local set_config(...,true) (platformAgentCatalog/index.ts:445, auditRetention.ts:235), confirming the gap is only that the trigger can't force malicious callers to do likewise. However, HIGH overstates it: the scenario is reachable only after the app is already compromised with table-level DELETE (a defense-in-depth control, no live injection vector shown), and in the default single-role deployment the app role owns the schema and could simply ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER — an equal or easier bypass — so the GUC is not the decisive weakness the finding implies. The proposed fix (revoke DELETE + SECURITY DEFINER + role separation) is a real hardening improvement, not a fix for an active bug, and only helps in a least-privilege deployment this repo does not ship. Net: a genuine but bounded hardening gap → MEDIUM.
decisiveEvidence: 0145_platform_db_hardening.sql:26-27 `IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' AND current_setting('lobe.allow_platform_audit_log_delete', true) = 'on'` — current_setting returns the same value for session-scoped SET as for SET LOCAL, so scope cannot be enforced by the trigger.
